cases.court: Supreme Court of Alabama
cases.holding: The Supreme Court restated the two-prong termination test - statutory grounds first, then consideration and rejection of all viable alternatives - and held that when a nonparent, including the State, is the petitioner it must additionally prove the child's dependency as a threshold matter.
cases.quote: if a nonparent, including the State, is the petitioner, then such a petitioner must meet the further threshold proof of dependency

relevance.DEC-05: Beasley fixes what the State must be prepared to prove when it files a dependency or termination petition: dependency as a threshold, plus statutory grounds.
relevance.OUT-02: Beasley is the controlling Alabama statement of the two-prong termination test that every Alabama TPR judgment is measured against.

cases.court: Supreme Court of Alabama
cases.holding: The Supreme Court reversed a termination judgment because the record did not clearly and convincingly show that the trial court had examined all viable alternatives, including relative placement and continued visitation, and remanded for that consideration.
cases.quote: the trial court also must find by clear and convincing evidence that there are no viable alternatives to the termination of parental rights

relevance.DEC-05: A petition that will end in termination must be built on a record of alternatives actually explored, because the viable-alternatives finding is reviewed de novo on the evidence.
relevance.OUT-01: The Court faulted DHR for having made no recent reunification effort and no current assessment of the mother, treating continued reunification work as part of the alternatives inquiry.
relevance.OUT-02: Ex parte T.V. is the modern Alabama Supreme Court application of Beasley's second prong and the case most often used to attack a termination judgment.
relevance.ACT-04: The Court pointed to the absence of any consideration of relative placement after the agency's mistaken belief that the placement was with a relative.
relevance.FAIL-03: The opinion notes DHR's affirmative duty to facilitate family reunification under the federal R.C. consent judgment, tying state practice to federal obligations.
relevance.PMC-01: The Court's reliance on DHR's federal-consent-decree reunification duty shows how federal monitoring obligations surface in individual Alabama appeals.

cases.court: Supreme Court of Alabama
cases.holding: The Court held that DHR employees sued over a foster placement in which the child was harmed were entitled to State-agent immunity because the plaintiffs produced no substantial evidence that the workers violated detailed mandatory rules - including DHR's relative-placement policy and foster-home minimum standards - or acted willfully or in bad faith.
cases.quote: We agree with the petitioners and hold that they satisfied their burden of establishing that they were entitled to State-agent immunity based on Ex parte Cranman.

relevance.ACT-03: The case tests foster-placement decisions against DHR's Minimum Standards for Foster Family Homes under the Cranman immunity framework.
relevance.ACT-04: The plaintiffs argued DHR's relative-placement policy was mandatory; the Court found no substantial evidence that the workers departed from it.
relevance.OUT-06: It is the controlling Alabama decision on personal liability of DHR staff when a child is seriously harmed in a placement they arranged.
relevance.FAIL-02: McClintock shows how far State-agent immunity shields removal and placement decisions absent proof of a violated checklist rule.
relevance.FAIL-04: It defines the plaintiff's evidentiary burden after harm to a child under agency supervision.
relevance.FAIL-05: A claim that the agency deviated from its own relative-placement policy fails without substantial evidence of the deviation.

cases.court: Supreme Court of Alabama
cases.holding: The Court held that a DHR service supervisor who, on receiving an intake report flagged for an immediate response, had no investigator available and instead confirmed the injured child would remain in the hospital over the weekend exercised protected supervisory judgment and was entitled to State-agent immunity.
cases.quote: The materials before us support a finding that Sumerlin did not ignore her responsibility; rather, she exercised her judgment in her supervisory capacity to deal with exigent circumstances.

relevance.INP-06: The case begins at hotline intake, where the report was coded for an immediate response.
relevance.INP-07: The report came from a hospital medical social worker who suspected non-accidental injuries.
relevance.INP-10: It addresses directly how an intake flagged for immediate response is escalated to an assigned investigator.
relevance.INP-12: The supervisor's protective step was to keep the child in a safe hospital environment rather than take custody.
relevance.DEC-01: Delay or deviation at the screening stage is measured against the DHR manual's response-time criteria.
relevance.DEC-02: The decision explains the manual's ninety-day initial-assessment window and the supervisory review it requires.
relevance.ACT-06: Continued hospitalization was used as the protective alternative to removal while the assessment was pending.
relevance.OUT-06: The child later died; the Court nonetheless found the supervisor's triage judgment immune.
relevance.FAIL-03: The plaintiff invoked the R.C. consent decree caseload standards, which the Court found not violated on the record.
relevance.PMC-02: The opinion details how DHR tracked and reported caseload compliance data to the state office under the consent decree.

cases.case_name: Brakefield v. Alabama Department of Human Resources
cases.court: Supreme Court of Alabama
cases.holding: The Court declined to overrule Mitchell v. Davis and held that foster parents are protected by parental immunity from simple-negligence claims by a foster child, so the negligence claims arising from the child's drowning were barred, while the wantonness claims could proceed.
cases.quote: negligence claims against the Spurgeons are barred by the doctrine of parental immunity

relevance.ACT-03: It fixes the civil-liability regime that attaches once a child is placed in an Alabama foster home.
relevance.OUT-04: Foster-parent immunity continues throughout the placement and shapes what remedies a youth leaving care may have.
relevance.OUT-06: This is the controlling Alabama decision on liability for a foster child's death in the foster home.
relevance.FAIL-04: Only wanton, not negligent, conduct by foster parents is actionable when a child dies under agency supervision.
relevance.PMC-04: The case illustrates the accountability gap that fatality review is meant to fill, since negligence claims are immunized.

cases.court: Supreme Court of Alabama
cases.holding: On rehearing the Court held that the trial court erred in terminating the father's parental rights because the evidence did not prove any applicable statutory ground, refused to terminate his rights, and remanded for a custody determination rather than ordering immediate transfer of the child.
cases.quote: the evidence in this case does not tend to prove any of Alabama's applicable statutory criteria for terminating the father's parental rights

relevance.DEC-05: Termination grounds in Alabama are purely statutory, so a petition must plead and prove one of them.
relevance.OUT-05: When the statutory criteria are not proved, the correct outcome is refusal to terminate and a remand on custody, not a compromise judgment.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit
cases.holding: The Eleventh Circuit held that due process permits a warrantless emergency removal where the totality of the circumstances shows objectively imminent danger to the child, rejecting the Second Circuit's rule that the availability of time to obtain a court order alone defeats the emergency exception.
cases.quote: We agree that the sole focus should not be whether there is time to obtain a court order.

relevance.INP-03: It supplies the federal constitutional standard officers and caseworkers in Alabama must meet before seizing a child without judicial authorization.
relevance.INP-12: This is the binding circuit standard governing protective custody taken before any court order.
relevance.DEC-04: It is the controlling authority in Alabama's circuit on when an emergency removal decision is constitutionally justified.
relevance.ACT-03: A placement that follows a warrantless removal is lawful only if the removal itself rested on objectively imminent danger.
relevance.ACT-05: The court balances protective intervention against the family's due-process interest in pre-deprivation process.
relevance.FAIL-02: It defines the constitutional line whose breach makes a removal actionable under 42 U.S.C. 1983 in the Eleventh Circuit.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment requires a State to support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence before it may sever the rights of parents in their natural child.
cases.quote: due process requires that the State support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence

relevance.INP-11: The opinion expressly notes that the Indian Child Welfare Act sets a still higher beyond-a-reasonable-doubt standard for terminating rights to an Indian child.
relevance.OUT-02: Santosky is the federal constitutional floor beneath Alabama's clear-and-convincing termination standard in Ala. Code 12-15-319.

cases.case_name: Lassiter v. Department of Social Services of Durham County
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that the Constitution does not require appointed counsel in every parental-termination proceeding and left the question whether due process requires counsel in a given case to the trial court in the first instance, subject to appellate review.
cases.quote: neither can we say that the Constitution requires the appointment of counsel in every parental termination proceeding

relevance.INP-12: It is the federal baseline against which Alabama's statutory right to counsel at the 72-hour shelter-care hearing must be read.
relevance.DEC-05: Lassiter governs whether a parent facing a petition has a constitutional as opposed to statutory claim to appointed counsel.
relevance.OUT-02: Alabama supplies appointed counsel in termination cases by statute; Lassiter marks the narrower constitutional floor.
relevance.FAIL-01: A counsel-based challenge to a termination judgment must satisfy Lassiter's case-by-case due-process inquiry.
relevance.FAIL-05: The case frames unequal access to counsel for indigent parents as a due-process rather than a categorical equal-protection question.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The plurality held that Washington's breathtakingly broad nonparental visitation statute was unconstitutional as applied because the court gave no special weight to a fit parent's determination of her children's best interests.
cases.quote: there is a presumption that fit parents act in the best interests of their children

relevance.INP-05: A parent who seeks help voluntarily remains presumptively fit, and that presumption governs how the agency may respond.
relevance.INP-12: State custody of a child taken from a fit parent must overcome the constitutional presumption in the parent's favor.
relevance.DEC-04: An emergency removal must rest on more than a judgment that the State could make a better decision than the parent.
relevance.ACT-05: Protective orders restricting a parent's contact must give special weight to the fit parent's own determinations.
relevance.FAIL-02: Troxel supplies the substantive due-process backdrop for wrongful-removal claims against state actors.
relevance.FAIL-05: Agency decisions that displace a fit parent's choices without special weight are constitutionally suspect.

cases.court: Court of Civil Appeals of Alabama
cases.holding: The court reversed a juvenile court's order transferring a dependency and termination case to the Chickasaw Nation tribal court because the transfer order addressed only one good-cause factor and was entered without an evidentiary hearing, and remanded for such a hearing under ICWA.
cases.quote: remand this matter to the juvenile court for it to conduct an evidentiary hearing on the motion to transfer pursuant to the ICWA

relevance.INP-11: This is Alabama's leading published decision on ICWA transfer to tribal court and the good-cause-to-the-contrary analysis.
relevance.ACT-04: The good-cause factors the court applied bear directly on where an Indian child may be placed and by which forum.

cases.case_name: N.G. v. Blount County Department of Human Resources
cases.court: Court of Civil Appeals of Alabama
cases.holding: The court affirmed dependency findings based on the mother's medication abuse and domestic violence and held that an indigent parent has no constitutional right to appointed counsel in a dependency proceeding, although Ala. Code 12-15-308(c) obliges the juvenile court to advise a parent of the right to counsel at the 72-hour shelter-care hearing and to investigate indigency.
cases.quote: an indigent parent does not have a constitutional right to the appointment of an attorney in a dependency proceeding

relevance.INP-04: The juvenile court's shelter-care duties under 12-15-308(c) start the judicial oversight cycle in a dependency case.
relevance.INP-12: It states what the juvenile court must do about counsel at the 72-hour hearing that follows emergency custody.
relevance.DEC-04: The case reviews a pickup order followed by a shelter-care hearing and shelter-care order maintaining DHR custody.
relevance.DEC-05: It applies the clear-and-convincing standard to the dependency adjudication that follows the petition.
relevance.ACT-05: Continued DHR custody rather than a protective order was upheld given the domestic violence and impairment evidence.

cases.case_name: T.J. v. Winston County Department of Human Resources
cases.court: Court of Civil Appeals of Alabama
cases.holding: The court held that the parents' conflict-based ineffective-assistance argument was not preserved because it was not specifically raised below, affirmed the termination, and explained that an unpreserved ineffective-assistance claim may instead be pursued by a Rule 60(b)(6) motion.
cases.quote: Ordinarily, to be preserved for appeal, a claim of ineffective assistance of counsel must be raised in a motion for a new trial.

relevance.ACT-02: The judgment under review relieved DHR of reasonable efforts and set adoption as the permanency plan, the usual sequel to failed court-ordered services.
relevance.OUT-05: It marks the procedural route by which a parent may reopen a case after the direct appeal closes.
relevance.FAIL-01: This is the Alabama rule on preserving and later raising ineffective assistance to overturn a termination judgment.

cases.case_name: P.S. v. Jefferson County Department of Human Resources
cases.court: Court of Civil Appeals of Alabama
cases.holding: The court reversed a termination judgment because DHR never identified the mother's parenting defect, never communicated what she needed to change, and was relieved of reasonable efforts when the child was five months old, so no clear and convincing evidence satisfied Ala. Code 12-15-319(a).
cases.quote: DHR did not provide the mother the opportunity to correct any conduct or condition that might have been a barrier to reunification with the child

relevance.DEC-06: The opinion shows what a front-end service response must contain before the case escalates to a petition.
relevance.ACT-01: Services are meaningless unless the agency first identifies and communicates the specific barrier to reunification.
relevance.ACT-02: Court-ordered service plans must be tailored to an identified parental defect that has been communicated to the parent.
relevance.OUT-01: Reunification cannot be declared impossible when the parent was never told what to fix.
relevance.OUT-05: Reversal and remand, not termination, is the outcome when DHR fails to meet 12-15-319(a).
relevance.FAIL-01: This is a clear example of appellate reversal of an agency-driven termination for evidentiary and reasonable-efforts failures.

cases.case_name: H.H. v. Baldwin County Department of Human Resources
cases.court: Court of Civil Appeals of Alabama
cases.holding: The court held that reasonable reunification efforts are excused when a parent has abandoned the child, but that a termination judgment cannot rest on that exception without an express juvenile-court finding of abandonment, and remanded for a specific finding as to whether and when abandonment occurred.
cases.quote: we agree with the general proposition that reasonable efforts to reunite a parent with a child are not required when a parent has abandoned the child

relevance.INP-05: The case began when a nonrelative caregiver contacted DHR about a child left without proper medication.
relevance.DEC-06: The opinion sets out DHR's general duty to use reasonable efforts before the case moves toward termination.
relevance.ACT-01: Rehabilitation services are ordinarily required whenever parental conditions prevent immediate reunification.
relevance.ACT-02: It is the leading Alabama statement of DHR's duty to use reasonable efforts to rehabilitate a parent and the narrow exceptions to it.
relevance.OUT-01: Reunification remains the statutory goal unless an aggravated circumstance such as abandonment is expressly found.
relevance.FAIL-01: An inconsistent or missing abandonment finding is itself a ground for appellate reversal and remand.

cases.case_name: Montgomery County Department of Human Resources v. A.S.N.
cases.court: Court of Civil Appeals of Alabama
cases.holding: The court reversed judgments declining to terminate parental rights, holding that the father had abandoned the children so no reasonable efforts were owed him, and that DHR had made reasonable efforts as to the mother, who failed to avail herself of the services offered.
cases.quote: DHR has no duty to make reasonable efforts to rehabilitate a parent who has abandoned his or her child

relevance.DEC-06: The opinion catalogues the transportation, employment, parenting-class and assessment services DHR offered before litigation.
relevance.ACT-01: It measures the adequacy of voluntary and offered services against the parent's own engagement with them.
relevance.ACT-02: The case defines how ISP goals and offered services are judged when the juvenile court finds efforts unreasonable.
relevance.OUT-01: Reunification efforts end where the parent abandons the child or refuses to use the services provided.

cases.case_name: Ex parte Limestone County Department of Human Resources
cases.court: Court of Civil Appeals of Alabama
cases.holding: The court held that after parental rights are terminated a juvenile court's permanency review under Ala. Code 12-15-321 is limited to reviewing DHR's efforts to achieve the permanency plan and does not empower the court to direct particular placements, but denied mandamus as to the orders refusing transcription.
cases.quote: the juvenile court exceeded its statutory authority and invaded DHR's authority insofar as it purported to override DHR's permanency plan by directing particular placements

relevance.INP-04: It marks the outer limit of what a juvenile court may order DHR to do on its own initiative.
relevance.INP-09: The juvenile court's finding that DHR failed to use reasonable efforts stands as oversight even though the placement directives were vacated.
relevance.ACT-02: Post-termination review is confined to whether DHR is using reasonable efforts to carry out its own plan.
relevance.ACT-03: Placement authority after termination rests with DHR under 12-15-320(b)(1), not with the court.
relevance.ACT-04: A court cannot compel a specific foster or sibling placement once permanent legal custody is with DHR.
relevance.OUT-03: It allocates decision-making authority over the permanency outcome between the juvenile court and DHR.
relevance.OUT-04: Children awaiting adoption remain under DHR's permanency authority subject only to reasonable-efforts review.
relevance.FAIL-01: The case shows mandamus as the vehicle for reversing a juvenile court order that exceeds statutory authority.
relevance.PMC-01: Section 12-15-321 permanency hearings are Alabama's in-case analogue to federal permanency oversight.
relevance.PMC-06: The opinion maps exactly where judicial review of agency permanency performance begins and ends.

cases.case_name: A.D.B.H. v. Houston County Department of Human Resources
cases.court: Court of Civil Appeals of Alabama
cases.holding: The court affirmed the termination, holding that the evidence supported the juvenile court's rejection of the maternal grandparents as a viable alternative given their prior custodial failures, the grandfather's deployment and the stepgrandmother's health.
cases.quote: The evidence supports the juvenile court's finding that awarding custody to the maternal grandparents was not a viable alternative to termination in the present case.

relevance.ACT-04: It shows the evidentiary basis on which Alabama courts accept or reject a relative as a placement resource.
relevance.OUT-02: The opinion applies Beasley's viable-alternatives prong where the proposed alternative is a relative placement.
relevance.OUT-03: Relative custody must be shown to be a workable permanency option, not merely available in theory.

cases.court: Court of Civil Appeals of Alabama
cases.holding: The court denied mandamus and upheld a protective order that, after in camera review, limited a parent's discovery of DHR child-abuse records in a dependency case to the names and information of expected witnesses, finding no abuse of discretion.
cases.quote: while this court has the authority to require a judge to exercise proper discretion, we cannot dictate the exercise of that discretion absent a showing of abuse

relevance.INP-01: Reporter identity is shielded in discovery to avoid discouraging the reporting of child abuse.
relevance.INP-02: Non-witness informants' names were protected from disclosure to the accused parent.
relevance.INP-06: It is the Alabama authority closest to confidentiality of hotline and informant identities.
relevance.DEC-03: A parent contesting a finding gets only records relevant and essential to the defense, after in camera review.
relevance.FAIL-06: The decision shows how narrowly Ala. Code 26-14-8 confidentiality is pierced even by a party in litigation.
relevance.PMC-03: Access to DHR case records for review purposes is controlled by 26-14-8's closed list of permitted uses.
relevance.PMC-05: It marks the statutory confidentiality wall that any transparency request for Alabama CPS records must cross.

cases.court: Supreme Court of Alabama
cases.holding: The Court held that although the Alabama Open Records Act carries a presumption in favor of disclosure, FERPA preempts it as to education records, so even redacted student financial-aid forms could not be released.
cases.quote: Because FERPA prohibits the very release of the redacted financial-aid forms and because FERPA takes precedence over the Open Records Act, the director is entitled to a summary judgment.

relevance.INP-08: School records bearing on a child are governed by FERPA, which limits what educators may disclose.
relevance.INP-09: Oversight bodies seeking agency records in Alabama run into the same federal-preemption limit.
relevance.DEC-03: Federal confidentiality statutes can override the state presumption of disclosure of agency findings.
relevance.FAIL-05: Redaction alone does not cure a federal statutory bar on disclosure.
relevance.FAIL-06: It is the governing Alabama Supreme Court statement on when the Open Records Act must yield to federal law.
relevance.PMC-02: Audit and accountability requests for state agency records are measured against this preemption analysis.
relevance.PMC-03: Citizen review bodies requesting records face the same Open Records Act presumption and its federal limits.
relevance.PMC-05: This is the controlling Alabama authority on the Open Records Act presumption of disclosure and its federal exceptions.
relevance.PMC-06: Any public dashboard built from Alabama agency data must respect the federal overrides recognized here.

cases.case_name: R.C. ex rel. Alabama Disabilities Advocacy Program v. Walley
cases.court: United States District Court for the Middle District of Alabama
cases.holding: The court granted the Commissioner's second motion to terminate the 1991 R.C. consent decree, finding that DHR had met both prongs of the termination clause by achieving and being able to sustain systemwide substantial compliance so that continued judicial oversight was no longer necessary.
cases.quote: DHR successfully has reformed its child welfare system by developing a system of care which substantially complies with the requirements of the Consent Decree and the Implementation Plan

relevance.INP-09: The R.C. court monitor's county-by-county reviews are the model for external audit of Alabama's CPS practice.
relevance.FAIL-03: This decision is the judicial record of Alabama's compliance posture under the consent decree that governed its child-welfare system from 1991 to 2007.
relevance.FAIL-06: The opinion catalogues the reporting and data obligations DHR carried under the decree and its implementation plan.
relevance.PMC-01: It is the only judicial determination of systemwide Alabama child-welfare performance and the closest analogue to CFSR review.
relevance.PMC-02: It explains the measurement framework, county ratings and performance reports DHR had to file.
relevance.PMC-03: The court monitor functioned as the independent reviewing body Alabama has otherwise lacked.
relevance.PMC-04: The decree's system-of-care standards were adopted after conditions the court called depraved, including harm to children in care.
relevance.PMC-05: The monitor's public reports are the principal published source of Alabama child-welfare performance data.
relevance.PMC-06: The substantial-compliance framework it applies is the benchmark against which later Alabama performance can be measured.

cases.case_name: Alabama Department of Human Resources v. B.V.
cases.court: Court of Civil Appeals of Alabama
cases.holding: The court affirmed the probate court's judgment allowing long-term foster parents to adopt a severely disabled young man the day after he turned nineteen, over DHR's objections to venue, consent and standing.
cases.quote: we conclude that the record contains substantial evidence supporting the Jefferson Probate Court's determination that B.V. and D.V.'s adoption of J.C. was in J.C.'s best interests

relevance.ACT-06: The child's profound medical and developmental needs framed every custody and care decision in the case.
relevance.OUT-03: It contrasts adoption with guardianship as the permanency route for a disabled person leaving DHR custody.
relevance.OUT-04: This is the Alabama decision closest on point to permanency for a foster youth at and beyond the age of majority, which in Alabama is nineteen.

cases.case_name: Randolph County Department of Human Resources v. A.H.
cases.court: Court of Civil Appeals of Alabama
cases.holding: The court affirmed the juvenile court's judgment denying DHR's dependency petition and returning the child to his parents, holding that DHR's abandonment theory was unpreserved and that it had not challenged the finding that the mother could provide the necessary care.
cases.quote: This court cannot consider an issue raised for the first time on appeal

relevance.INP-04: The juvenile court's independent assessment of dependency is the check on an agency referral.
relevance.INP-05: The family kept the child after a crisis involving suicidal ideation, showing that agency involvement need not end in custody.
relevance.DEC-01: A juvenile court may reject DHR's dependency theory outright and close the case.
relevance.DEC-05: It shows what happens when a filed dependency petition is not supported by evidence of dependency.
relevance.OUT-05: This is a published Alabama example of dismissal of a dependency petition and return of the child to the parents.
relevance.FAIL-01: The decision illustrates judicial rejection of an agency custody request and the preservation rules that govern its appeal.

cases.court: Supreme Court of Alabama
cases.holding: The Court denied State-agent immunity to the CA/N investigator, who never made the home visit required by Ala. Admin. Code r. 660-5-34-.05(1)(b), and to the ongoing worker, who ignored her supervisor's binding written instructions, but granted immunity to the two supervisors whose duties involved judgment.
cases.quote: because Watson has not submitted substantial evidence indicating that she complied with subsection (b), Watson has not demonstrated that she is entitled to State-agent immunity

relevance.INP-01: A report of physical abuse to a child triggers the mandatory assessment standards in the DHR administrative regulations.
relevance.INP-03: The investigation followed a hospital-sourced abuse report and had to meet the regulation's contact requirements.
relevance.INP-07: The case arose from injuries documented at Children's Hospital that the ongoing worker never obtained records for.
relevance.INP-10: It identifies the specific regulatory steps that convert an accepted report into a compliant assessment.
relevance.DEC-01: An assessment closed without the required home visit cannot support a protected screening judgment.
relevance.DEC-02: Ala. Admin. Code r. 660-5-34-.05(1) sets standards for conducting CA/N assessments that must be followed.
relevance.DEC-03: The plaintiff challenged the worker's entry of an indicated disposition where unable to complete was the accurate one.
relevance.DEC-04: The child was released to the mother's custody without the required home visit and later died.
relevance.OUT-06: This is the controlling Alabama case on worker liability for a child's death after a defective investigation.
relevance.FAIL-04: It shows precisely which regulatory omissions defeat immunity when a child dies under agency supervision.
relevance.PMC-04: The opinion is a detailed judicial post-mortem of the agency failures preceding a child fatality.

cases.court: Supreme Court of Alabama
cases.holding: The Court restated the rule governing State-agent immunity into five categories of protected conduct subject to two exceptions - conduct that federal or state law requires otherwise, and conduct that is willful, malicious, fraudulent, in bad faith, beyond authority or under a mistaken interpretation of law - and held that university physicians treating a student fell within no protected category and so were not immune.
cases.quote: when the State agent acts willfully, maliciously, fraudulently, in bad faith, beyond his or her authority, or under a mistaken interpretation of the law

relevance.DEC-01: A screening or closure decision is protected only if it is genuine judgment within a Cranman category and free of bad faith.
relevance.DEC-02: Category (3) protects a worker discharging duties imposed by statute, rule or regulation only when the rule prescribes the manner and the worker performs the duties in that manner.
relevance.FAIL-02: Cranman's first exception withholds immunity whenever the Constitution or laws of the United States require otherwise, which is the doorway for a constitutional wrongful-removal claim against an Alabama caseworker.
relevance.FAIL-04: This is the source of the standard every Alabama child-fatality suit against DHR staff is measured by, including Ex parte Watson and Ex parte McClintock.
relevance.FAIL-05: A retaliatory or discriminatory act by a State agent is outside immunity because it is willful, malicious or in bad faith under the restated exception.

cases.court: Supreme Court of Alabama
cases.holding: The Court adopted the Cranman plurality's restated State-agent immunity test as the holding of the Court and denied the employees' mandamus petition because the families might still prove that an employee failed to discharge duties pursuant to detailed rules such as a checklist or acted willfully, maliciously, fraudulently, in bad faith, beyond authority or under a mistaken interpretation of law.
cases.quote: We today adopt this new test suggested in Cranman.

relevance.DEC-02: Butts is what makes the Cranman categories binding law, so a caseworker's compliance with the DHR manual's assessment standards is judged under a test the whole Court has adopted.
relevance.FAIL-04: It is the decision that supplies the checklist exception later used to deny immunity to the workers in Gowens and Ex parte Watson after children were killed or injured.

cases.court: Supreme Court of Alabama
cases.holding: After six foster children died in a foster-home fire the Court held that parental immunity extends in qualified form to foster parents and to the DHR commissioner, county director and case supervisor standing in loco parentis, barring simple-negligence but not wantonness claims, and that the county DHR itself is a State agency absolutely immune under Article I, section 14.
cases.quote: we hold that foster parents may assert the defense of parental immunity against claims of simple negligence brought by foster children in their care

relevance.ACT-03: It sets the liability rules that attach the moment a child is placed in an Alabama foster home, and holds the county DHR itself absolutely immune from suit.
relevance.OUT-06: This is the foundational Alabama decision on who can be sued when foster children die in care, and it is the rule Brakefield later declined to overrule.
relevance.FAIL-04: It draws the negligence/wantonness line that determines whether any damages remedy survives a child's death under agency supervision.

cases.court: Supreme Court of Alabama
cases.holding: The Court reversed and held that a parent, who has a right to appointed counsel in a termination case, may raise a claim of ineffective assistance of that counsel by a Rule 60(b)(6) motion filed within a reasonable time, and that a motion filed within sixty days after the Court of Civil Appeals affirmed the termination was timely.
cases.quote: In a parental-rights-termination case, a parent has a right to appointed counsel.

relevance.OUT-02: It is the Alabama Supreme Court's statement of the right to appointed counsel that accompanies every termination judgment, and the authority behind the effective-assistance rule Alabama courts apply.
relevance.OUT-05: It identifies the Rule 60(b)(6) motion as the means of reopening a closed termination case when the ordinary fourteen-day postjudgment window was practically unusable.
relevance.FAIL-01: This is the source decision behind T.J. v. Winston County DHR and the brief's practice point: an ineffective-assistance attack on a termination judgment survives the direct appeal through Rule 60(b)(6).

cases.court: United States District Court for the Middle District of Alabama
cases.holding: A three-judge court held Alabama's summary child-removal statute unconstitutional, ruling that removing a child from a parent without prior notice and a hearing violates procedural due process absent immediate or threatened harm, that a post-seizure hearing must follow as soon as practicable, and that the statute's welfare and neglect standards were unconstitutionally vague.
cases.quote: this Court is of the opinion that Alabama Code Title 13, § 352(4) violates the procedural due process clause of the Fourteenth Amendment

relevance.INP-03: The removal at issue was carried out by a Montgomery police officer on a juvenile judge's summary pickup direction, which is the law-enforcement referral pathway the court held unconstitutional as applied.
relevance.INP-12: It is the origin of Alabama's rule that protective custody without prior notice and hearing is lawful only on immediate or threatened harm to the child.
relevance.DEC-04: The court found no emergency where the child was clothed, clean and unharmed and the home was clean and stocked with food, which is the factual benchmark for an unjustified emergency removal in Alabama.
relevance.ACT-05: The decision requires that intrusion into the family be preceded by notice and an opportunity for rebuttal before an impartial tribunal unless exigent circumstances exist.
relevance.FAIL-02: It is the closest published Alabama-specific authority on unlawful removal and the source of the exigency standard later expressed in Eleventh Circuit law.

cases.court: Supreme Court of Alabama
cases.holding: The Court affirmed summary judgment for a photo shop that reported nude photographs of a child to the FBI, holding that the report rested on reasonable cause under the permissive-reporting provision of Ala. Code 26-14-4 and was therefore immune under 26-14-9, and that the reporter had no duty to include the parent's innocent explanation in the report.
cases.quote: because the report was based on "reasonable cause," the statute exempts Van's Photo from liability in making the report

relevance.INP-02: This is the leading Alabama application of Ala. Code 26-14-4, which lets any person - not only a mandated reporter - report on reasonable cause to suspect abuse or neglect.
relevance.INP-06: It shows what protects an ordinary citizen or business that calls in a suspicion: reasonable cause at the time of the call, not whether the suspicion proves out.

cases.court: Supreme Court of Alabama
cases.holding: The Court affirmed summary judgment on outrage and family-interference claims brought against defendants alleged to have induced others to make false child-abuse reports, holding that the pre-1998 version of Ala. Code 26-14-9 gave absolute immunity because the claimed injury related directly to the reporting of suspected child abuse.
cases.quote: We conclude that the plaintiffs' claim of intentional infliction of emotional distress relates directly to these defendants' alleged reporting of suspected child abuse.

relevance.INP-02: It is the decision that made a knowingly false third-party report unactionable under the old statute, and it is the reason the Legislature added the good-faith requirement to 26-14-9 in 1998.
relevance.INP-06: A practitioner testing a bad-faith hotline call needs this before-and-after line: absolute immunity under Evans, good-faith-qualified immunity after the 1998 amendment.

cases.court: Supreme Court of Alabama
cases.holding: The Court affirmed dismissal of a patient's claims against the psychologists who reported his admitted abuse of two children, holding that reasonable cause to suspect abuse both authorizes a permissive report under Ala. Code 26-14-4 and satisfies the good-faith condition on immunity in 26-14-9 as amended in 1998, and that 26-14-9 impliedly repeals the psychotherapist-patient privilege to that extent.
cases.quote: Under the permissive reporting provision of § 26-14-4, the existence of reasonable cause triggers the authority to make a report.

relevance.INP-01: It is the modern Alabama Supreme Court statement of the immunity that accompanies the mandatory-reporting scheme in Ala. Code 26-14-3 and its permissive counterpart.
relevance.INP-02: Marks fixes the good-faith standard that now governs every voluntary or third-party report in Alabama: reasonable cause at the time of the report.
relevance.INP-06: It holds that the good-faith condition attaches to the basis for the report, not to how the reporter dealt with the suspected perpetrator, which is what protects a hotline caller.
relevance.INP-07: The Court held that a psychotherapist's disclosure of a patient's admitted child abuse is immune notwithstanding the psychotherapist-patient privilege.

cases.court: Supreme Court of Alabama
cases.holding: The Court affirmed dismissal of a grandmother's claims against an emergency-room physician who reported a suspected abusive burn that DHR later found unsubstantiated, holding that a mandated reporter acting within the requirements of the Child Abuse Reporting Act has absolute immunity under Ala. Code 26-14-9 where no injury unrelated to the reporting is alleged.
cases.quote: Because the action of Dr. Pound and the Decatur Medical Surgical Center were within the requirements of the Child Abuse Reporting Act, § 26-14-9 provides them with absolute immunity.

relevance.INP-01: This is the controlling Alabama decision on what a mandated reporter under Ala. Code 26-14-3 risks by reporting - nothing, so long as the report is what the Act requires.
relevance.INP-07: The report originated in a hospital emergency room from a physician's examination of a burn, the paradigm medical disclosure, and the Court held the resulting investigation gave the family no claim.

cases.case_name: Gowens v. Tys. S. ex rel. Davis
cases.court: Supreme Court of Alabama
cases.holding: The Court held that a DHR investigator was not protected by Ala. Code 26-14-9, which covers reporting rather than investigating, and was not entitled to Cranman State-agent immunity because the DHR Manual's investigation standards required him to verify from an outside source how many children were in the household and to interview them, leaving him no judgment to exercise; it also held he owed the uninterviewed children a duty.
cases.quote: The mandates of the DHR Manual in this regard are precisely the sort of "detailed rules or regulations" that State agents cannot ignore, except at their peril.

relevance.INP-10: It identifies the specific DHR Manual steps - verifying the number of children in the home from an outside source and interviewing each of them - that convert an accepted CA/N report into a compliant investigation.
relevance.DEC-01: An investigation closed without verifying who actually lives in the home is not a protected exercise of screening judgment.
relevance.DEC-02: This is the Alabama Supreme Court's core application of the checklist exception to the DHR Manual's standards for completing an investigation.
relevance.OUT-06: The uninterviewed children were later caught in a house fire; Gowens is the decision holding an investigator personally answerable for that outcome.
relevance.FAIL-02: It establishes that the reporting immunity in 26-14-9 does not extend to an agency employee's investigation and removal decisions, leaving those exposed under Cranman.

cases.court: Court of Civil Appeals of Alabama
cases.holding: The court affirmed dependency judgments but held that Ala. Code 26-14-8(b)(8), which permits otherwise confidential child-abuse reports to be used by an attorney representing a child or a parent, applies equally in dependency cases as a matter of due process when the information is relevant at the adjudicatory phase, and that refusing to disclose informant names here was error but harmless because no relevancy was shown.
cases.quote: We consider it equally applicable to child dependency cases because it represents nothing more than due process when it is relevant information in the adjudicatory phase of the proceedings.

relevance.DEC-03: This is the rule Alabama parents actually rely on to see the CA/N reports behind a finding: counsel may use the confidential record when it is relevant at adjudication.
relevance.FAIL-06: It supplies the affirmative half of Ala. Code 26-14-8 - the statute is a confidentiality rule with a built-in litigation exception, not an absolute bar.
relevance.PMC-03: Any review or oversight use of Alabama CPS records is measured against 26-14-8's closed list of permitted uses, of which subsection (b)(8) is one.
relevance.PMC-05: Ex parte Smith is a gloss on this decision; a transparency request must start from Lawler's rule and Smith's limits on it.

cases.case_name: V.M. v. State Dept. of Human Resources
cases.court: Court of Civil Appeals of Alabama
cases.holding: The court reversed judgments terminating a mother's parental rights as premature, holding that she had accomplished all but one DHR goal and had been sober for nearly a year so that her ongoing rehabilitation was itself a viable alternative, that the maternal grandmother had never been evaluated as a relative resource, and that DHR carries an affirmative duty to facilitate reunification under the federal consent judgment.
cases.quote: Pursuant to the terms of a consent judgment in federal litigation, DHR has an affirmative duty to facilitate family reunification whenever that goal is possible.

relevance.ACT-02: This is the source of the frequently quoted rule that DHR's reunification obligation is affirmative and federally grounded, not discretionary, once a service plan is in place.
relevance.ACT-04: The court held that a grandmother who had asked to be considered since 1995 but was never given a home evaluation remained an unexplored relative resource.
relevance.OUT-01: A parent who is visibly working the plan cannot be written off; reunification remained the required goal while the mother was still completing her last goal.
relevance.FAIL-03: It is the state-court decision that enforces the R.C. consent decree's reunification requirement inside an individual Alabama termination appeal, and the authority Ex parte T.V. builds on.

cases.court: Court of Civil Appeals of Alabama
cases.holding: The court affirmed the denial of the parents' Rule 60(b) motions to set aside a dependency judgment, holding that any failure to appoint counsel for the indigent mother implicated only a statutory right under Ala. Code 12-15-305(b) and not constitutional due process, so the judgment was not void and could be challenged only by appeal.
cases.quote: if the juvenile court erred by not appointing counsel for the mother, as an indigent parent, that error affected only a statutory right and not a constitutional due-process right

relevance.INP-12: It is the authority N.G. relies on for the rule governing counsel after emergency custody: the juvenile court's duty to advise and appoint is statutory, so a breach does not void the shelter-care or dependency judgment.
relevance.DEC-05: A parent contesting a dependency petition has a statutory, not constitutional, claim to appointed counsel, and the remedy for its denial is a timely appeal rather than a collateral attack.

cases.case_name: Payne v. State Department of Human Resources
cases.court: Court of Civil Appeals of Alabama
cases.holding: The court reversed a CHINS adjudication initiated by a school superintendent, holding that the juvenile court abused its discretion by denying a continuance where the child's guardian ad litem was given only forty-five minutes to examine the school records that were the sole evidence, defeating the statutory opportunity to examine and controvert written reports under Ala. Code 12-15-65(f).
cases.quote: Because a reasonable opportunity was not allowed for preparation of the defense of the accused in this case, we find the court to have abused its judicial discretion.

relevance.INP-04: The petition was filed by a school official and prosecuted by the district attorney, showing how a school referral becomes a juvenile-court case in Alabama.
relevance.INP-08: This is the published Alabama decision closest to an educational disclosure: a school superintendent's petition supported entirely by school records and testimony from the assistant principal.
relevance.DEC-03: The opinion states what a family is owed before school or agency records can be used to support a finding against a child: notice and a real opportunity to examine and controvert them.

cases.case_name: Ex parte Montgomery County Department of Human Resources
cases.court: Court of Civil Appeals of Alabama
cases.holding: The court held that a juvenile court acted within its authority to review the service plan for a multiple-needs child under Ala. Code 12-15-71(h)(1) when, after finding that a deaf and disabled dependent girl had been mistreated and over-medicated following DHR's transfer, it rescinded the transfer and ordered her returned to the prior facility and therapist, but granted mandamus as to the portion of the order requiring the State to pay the private placement's cost.
cases.quote: the juvenile court did not dictate to DHR how it was to care for D.R.S. without first giving DHR the opportunity to carry out its legislative mandate

relevance.INP-04: It defines what a juvenile court may do on its own motion when it concludes that the care a State agency is providing a child in its custody is harming her.
relevance.ACT-02: Section 12-15-71(h)(1) gives the juvenile court authority to review and rescind the service plan for a multiple-needs child, the pre-termination counterpart to the narrow post-termination review in Ex parte Limestone County DHR.
relevance.ACT-03: A court may restore a child to a prior placement it finds appropriate, but it may not order the State - as opposed to the county - to pay for a private facility.
relevance.ACT-06: This is Alabama's fullest published treatment of emergency and ongoing medical and psychiatric care for a dependent child, including over-medication and the reinstatement of a specific therapist.

cases.case_name: R.C. ex rel. Alabama Disabilities Advocacy Program v. Nachman
cases.court: United States District Court for the Middle District of Alabama
cases.holding: The court denied DHR's Rule 60(b) motion to vacate or modify the 1991 R.C. consent decree, rejecting the claims of collusion, lack of class standing and change of law, finding that DHR came to the court without clean hands and that substantial compliance with the decree's system of care remained a distant goal.
cases.quote: The consent decree in this case came about because DHR would not or could not comply with constitutional, federal statutory and common-law mandates.

relevance.INP-09: It describes the court monitor's role as the court's agent assessing DHR's compliance county by county, which is the external-oversight machinery Alabama otherwise lacks.
relevance.FAIL-03: This is the decision that construes and enforces the substantive requirements of the decree that governed Alabama DHR from 1991 to 2007, as distinct from the 2007 exit ruling in Walley.
relevance.PMC-01: It sets out the goals, operating principles, standards and phased county-by-county implementation plan against which Alabama's systemwide performance was actually measured.
relevance.PMC-02: The opinion records the monitor's status reports on hiring freezes, inadequate funding and reduced training as documented compliance deficiencies.
relevance.PMC-03: The court-appointed monitor functioned as the independent reviewing body whose reports are the closest Alabama analogue to a citizen review panel.

cases.case_name: J.V. v. Marshall Cnty. Dep't of Human Res. (Ex parte Marshall Cnty. Dep't of Human Res.)
cases.court: Court of Civil Appeals of Alabama
cases.holding: The court denied DHR's mandamus petition in its entirety, holding that DHR had shown no clear legal right to cancellation of the father's evidentiary hearing and none to transcription of two hearings it had not shown were evidentiary, and noting that the former Rule 20(B) language requiring transcription on a paying party's request no longer exists.
cases.quote: Because DHR is unable to establish that it has a clear, legal right to the relief it seeks in this petition, we deny the petition.

relevance.INP-04: It is the current statement of what a party - including DHR - must show before an appellate court will direct a juvenile court to hold or cancel a hearing or to produce a record.
relevance.PMC-06: This is the companion authority Ex parte Limestone County DHR relies on for the modern transcript rule, and it shows how thin the paper trail of juvenile-court oversight can lawfully be.

notes: Every case in this brief was retrieved from CourtListener during this session and its opinion text read. All quotes are exact substrings of the majority/lead opinion text (whitespace and curly quotes normalized) and none exceeds 30 words.

The existing layers.case_law.key_cases entries in the AL node files are keyword-matched noise - recent certiorari dockets and slip listings with synthetic citations. None was retained; every title was looked up and none was on point for the doctrine its node turns on.

Troxel v. Granville: the quoted sentence is from Justice O'Connor's opinion announcing the judgment of the Court (a four-Justice plurality). It is not a dissent or a concurrence in the judgment, but lawyers should cite it as the Troxel plurality.

H.H. v. Baldwin County DHR is published at 989 So. 2d 1094 as a single opinion containing the original October 5, 2007 opinion and the March 14, 2008 opinion on return to remand. The quote is from the majority portion of the original opinion; CourtListener dates the cluster 2008-03-14.

R.C. ex rel. Alabama Disabilities Advocacy Program v. Walley is a federal district court decision (M.D. Ala.), below the preference hierarchy. It is included because it is the only judicial determination of Alabama's systemwide child-welfare performance - the 1991 R.C. consent decree governed Alabama DHR practice until this 2007 termination order - and there is no Alabama appellate or Eleventh Circuit authority on CFSR/Title IV-E compliance. Ex parte T.V. and Williford v. Toole both apply the decree's substantive requirements in state court.
No unpublished memorandum decisions were used. Every entry is a published opinion (CourtListener status: Published).

Gap - Fourth Amendment caseworker entry, home searches and child interviews at school: no published Alabama appellate decision was found. The federal standard from Doe v. Kearney (11th Cir.), binding in Alabama, is supplied at INP-12, DEC-04, ACT-03 and FAIL-02. Alabama practice is instead litigated through Cranman State-agent immunity (Gowens, Ex parte Watson, Ex parte McClintock), not through Section 1983 - no published Eleventh Circuit or Alabama appellate Section 1983 wrongful-removal damages case against Alabama DHR workers was located.

Gap - substantiated/'indicated' findings and the central registry: Ala. Code 26-14-7.1 gives the full adversarial hearing only to persons connected with a facility, agency or home that cares for children; a parent investigated at home gets only an administrative record review. No published Alabama appellate decision squarely adjudicating a parent's due-process challenge to an 'indicated' disposition was found. Ex parte Smith (records/discovery), Ex parte Watson (challenge to an 'indicated' disposition entered where 'unable to complete' was accurate) and Kendrick (confidentiality/preemption) are the nearest authority. Fred V. v. Miss Emma's Day Care Home, 959 So. 2d 51 (Ala. 2006), construes Ala. Code 26-14-8(c)(1) confidentiality but only on rehearing of a mandamus petition and states no rule in quotable form, so it was not included.

Gap - differential response / alternative response (DEC-06): Alabama has no published appellate decision on a formal DR track. The node is served by the reasonable-efforts and services cases (H.H., P.S., Montgomery County DHR v. A.S.N.), which state what front-end service work must contain.

Gap - extended foster care past 18 (OUT-04): Alabama's age of majority is 19 (Ala. Code 26-1-1) and no published Alabama decision construes the Chafee Foster Care Independence Act or the FCSIAA extension to 21. Alabama DHR v. B.V. (adoption of a disabled former foster youth the day after he turned 19) is the closest published authority; Brakefield and Ex parte Limestone County DHR supply the surrounding placement and permanency-authority rules.
Gap - children missing from care: no published Alabama appellate decision was located on runaway or missing children from foster placements.

Gap - discrimination and retaliation (FAIL-05): no published Alabama or Eleventh Circuit decision was found applying MEPA, the Interethnic Adoption Provisions, Title VI or the ADA to Alabama placement or investigation decisions, and no Alabama reporter-retaliation case was found. The node is served by the general constitutional and immunity framework (Troxel, Lassiter, Ex parte McClintock, Kendrick, and now Ex parte Cranman, whose willful/malicious/bad-faith exception is the only Alabama route to personal liability for a retaliatory act by a State agent); this is flagged as a genuine hole rather than authority on the point.

Gaps - PMC-02 through PMC-06: there is no Alabama case law on CAPTA Citizen Review Panels, on the Protect Our Kids Act fatality commission, or on OIG/Single Audit Act findings. Those nodes are served by R.C. v. Nachman and R.C. v. Walley (the only judicial systemwide monitoring record), Kendrick (Alabama Open Records Act presumption and its federal limits) and Ex parte Smith with In Matter of Lawler (Ala. Code 26-14-8 confidentiality and its litigation exception), which together define what a transparency or oversight request in Alabama can and cannot reach.

Case-name styling: CourtListener's cluster names are used. Two mandamus proceedings are styled in the reporter under the underlying action - Williford v. Toole, 26 So. 3d 1178, is Yvonne Sumerlin's mandamus petition, and Brakefield v. Alabama Department of Human Resources, 82 So. 3d 663, is the Spurgeons' mandamus petition. Practitioners may see these cited as Ex parte Sumerlin and Ex parte Spurgeon.

Alabama has no state ICWA. Only two published Alabama ICWA opinions were located (Ex parte C.L.J. on transfer/good cause, J.N.T. on Section 1912(a) notice). No published Alabama decision construes ICWA active efforts, the qualified expert witness requirement, or the Section 1915 placement preferences; Santosky notes ICWA's higher beyond-a-reasonable-doubt standard for termination.

Practice point for families: in Alabama the two-prong Beasley test controls every termination. When DHR or another nonparent petitions, it must prove dependency AND that no viable alternative exists, both by clear and convincing evidence (Ex parte Beasley; Ex parte T.V.). Relative placement and maintaining the status quo are the alternatives most often litigated (A.D.B.H.; Ex parte T.V.; V.M.).

Practice point for counsel: an ineffective-assistance claim must be raised in a motion for a new trial within the 14-day period of Rule 1(B), Ala. R. Juv. P., or, if the transcript is unavailable, by a Rule 60(b)(6) motion filed within a reasonable time (Ex parte E.D.; T.J. v. Winston County DHR). There is a statutory right to counsel in termination cases but no constitutional right to appointed counsel in a dependency case (Ex parte E.D.; T.L. v. W.C.L.; N.G. v. Blount County DHR; Lassiter).

Added Ex parte Cranman, 792 So. 2d 392 (Ala. 2000), for DEC-01, DEC-02, FAIL-02, FAIL-04 and FAIL-05: it is the source of the State-agent immunity test that Gowens, Ex parte Watson, Williford and Ex parte McClintock all apply, and the brief previously relied on the doctrine without citing it. Caution for citation: the restatement is a plurality (Hooper, C.J., and Houston, J., concurring; Johnstone, J., concurring specially; Cook and Brown, JJ., concurring in the judgment; Maddox and See, JJ., dissenting); it is citable only because Ex parte Butts adopted it. The CourtListener cluster is dated 2000-11-22 because the November 24, 1999 opinion was withdrawn and this opinion substituted on rehearing.

Added Ex parte Butts, 775 So. 2d 173 (Ala. 2000), for DEC-02 and FAIL-04: it adopted the Cranman restatement as the holding of the Court and is the source of the 'checklist' formulation quoted in Ex parte McClintock, Ex parte Watson and Gowens.

Added Mitchell v. Davis, 598 So. 2d 801 (Ala. 1992), for ACT-03, OUT-06 and FAIL-04: it is the foster-parent parental-immunity rule Brakefield declined to overrule and the holding that a county DHR is a State agency absolutely immune under Article I, section 14, without which Brakefield is unintelligible.

Added Ex parte E.D., 777 So. 2d 113 (Ala. 2000), for OUT-02, OUT-05 and FAIL-01: it is the Alabama Supreme Court source of the right to appointed counsel in a termination case and of the Rule 60(b)(6) route for a later ineffective-assistance claim that T.J. v. Winston County DHR rests on. Note for accuracy: the 'right to effective assistance' language the brief's practice point uses originates in Crews v. Houston County Dep't of Pensions & Security, 358 So. 2d 451 (Ala. Civ. App. 1978), which Ex parte E.D. quotes; the quote used here is the Supreme Court's own sentence.

Added Roe v. Conn, 417 F. Supp. 769 (M.D. Ala. 1976), for INP-03, INP-12, DEC-04, ACT-05 and FAIL-02: a three-judge M.D. Ala. court struck down Alabama's summary-removal statute and required pre-removal notice and hearing absent immediate or threatened harm, which is the origin of Alabama's exigency standard and the closest Alabama-specific wrongful-removal authority; it directly fills the brief's own admitted DEC-04/FAIL-02 gap. It is a federal district court decision and therefore below the preference hierarchy, but the statutes it struck down (Ala. Code tit. 13, sections 350 and 352) have since been replaced by the 1975 juvenile code, so it is cited for the constitutional standard rather than for current statutory text.

Added Hall v. Van's Photo, Inc., 595 So. 2d 1368 (Ala. 1992), for INP-02 and INP-06: the earlier application of the reasonable-cause standard under the permissive-reporting provision, Ala. Code 26-14-4, that Marks builds on.

Added Evans v. Waddell, 689 So. 2d 23 (Ala. 1997), for INP-02 and INP-06: it construed the pre-1998 version of Ala. Code 26-14-9 to give absolute immunity even to defendants alleged to have induced false reports, and prompted the 1998 'good faith' amendment; without it the good-faith qualification in Marks has no history.

Added Marks v. Tenbrunsel, 910 So. 2d 1255 (Ala. 2005), for INP-01, INP-02, INP-06 and INP-07: it is the modern Alabama Supreme Court statement of the good-faith condition on reporter immunity and of the relationship between mandatory reporting and the psychotherapist-patient privilege. INP-01 and INP-02 previously had no on-point authority at all. The main opinion is by Woodall, J.; Stuart, J., dissented as to Dr. Tenbrunsel and Parker, J., concurred in the result in part - the quote used is from the main opinion.

Added Brown v. Pound, 585 So. 2d 885 (Ala. 1991), for INP-01 and INP-07: the controlling Alabama decision that an emergency-room physician who reports a suspected abusive injury as Ala. Code 26-14-3 requires has absolute immunity under 26-14-9, which is the rule every mandated medical reporter in Alabama relies on.

Added Gowens v. Tys. S. ex rel. Davis, 948 So. 2d 513 (Ala. 2006), for INP-10, DEC-01, DEC-02, OUT-06 and FAIL-02: it is the leading Alabama decision holding that the DHR Manual's investigation standards are mandatory 'detailed rules' that defeat State-agent immunity, that the reporting immunity in 26-14-9 does not cover an agency employee's investigation, and that an investigator owes a duty to children he failed to interview. The brief named Gowens in its notes but never cited it.

Added In Matter of Lawler, 484 So. 2d 451 (Ala. Civ. App. 1986), for DEC-03, FAIL-06, PMC-03 and PMC-05: it is the rule that Ex parte Smith glosses - Ala. Code 26-14-8(b)(8) lets a parent's or child's attorney use otherwise confidential CA/N records when they are relevant at the adjudicatory phase. Correction to the verifier's citation: the decision was released February 7, 1986 (cert. quashed at 484 So. 2d 455 (Ala. 1986)), not 1985.

Added V.M. v. State Dept. of Human Resources, 710 So. 2d 915 (Ala. Civ. App. 1998), for ACT-02, ACT-04, OUT-01 and FAIL-03: it is the source of the rule that DHR carries an affirmative, federally grounded duty to facilitate family reunification, the rule Ex parte T.V. later invoked. Note: the 'last and most extreme disposition permitted by statute' language the brief attributes to V.M. is V.M.'s quotation of East v. Meadows, 529 So. 2d 1010, 1012 (Ala. Civ. App. 1988), so the quote used here is V.M.'s own sentence instead.

Added T.L. v. W.C.L. for INP-12 and DEC-05: it is the decision N.G. v. Blount County DHR relies on for the proposition that an indigent parent has no constitutional right to appointed counsel in a dependency proceeding. Correction to the verifier's citation: the official reporter citation is 203 So. 3d 66, not 208 So. 3d 66, and the decision was released January 8, 2016.

Added R.C. ex rel. Alabama Disabilities Advocacy Program v. Nachman, 969 F. Supp. 682 (M.D. Ala. 1997), for INP-09, FAIL-03, PMC-01, PMC-02 and PMC-03: it construes the substantive requirements of the R.C. consent decree that governed Alabama DHR from 1991 to 2007 and describes the monitor, the implementation plan and the county-conversion schedule, where the brief previously cited only the 2007 exit ruling in Walley. Like Walley it is a federal district court decision, included for the same reason.

Added J.V. v. Marshall Cnty. Dep't of Human Res. (Ex parte Marshall Cnty. Dep't of Human Res.), 252 So. 3d 1098 (Ala. Civ. App. 2017), for INP-04 and PMC-06: it is the companion authority Ex parte Limestone County DHR relies on for the modern Rule 20, Ala. R. Juv. P., transcript rule, and it records that the former mandatory-transcription language no longer exists. CourtListener styles the cluster under the underlying appeal; the reporter and practitioners cite it as Ex parte Marshall County Department of Human Resources. It is a different proceeding from Ex parte Marshall County Department of Human Resources, 233 So. 3d 345 (Ala. 2017).

Added Payne v. State Department of Human Resources, 532 So. 2d 1263 (Ala. Civ. App. 1988), for INP-04, INP-08 and DEC-03: INP-08 previously had no case at all. No published Alabama appellate decision was found on an educator's duty to report suspected abuse to DHR or on liability for failing to do so; Payne (a CHINS petition filed by a school superintendent and proved entirely by school records) and Kendrick (FERPA preemption of the Open Records Act as to student records) are the nearest published Alabama authority, and this is flagged as a genuine hole rather than authority on the reporting duty itself. Ala. Code 26-14-3 lists school teachers and officials among mandated reporters, and Brown v. Pound states the immunity that attaches to their reports.

Added Ex parte Montgomery County Department of Human Resources, 10 So. 3d 31 (Ala. Civ. App. 2008), for INP-04, ACT-02, ACT-03 and ACT-06: ACT-06 previously had only one case. It is Alabama's fullest published treatment of medical and psychiatric care for a dependent child - a deaf, diabetic and mentally ill teenager transferred out of a specialist academy and then over-medicated and mistreated - and of the juvenile court's power under Ala. Code 12-15-71(h)(1) to rescind a State agency's service plan, subject to the separation-of-powers limit that only the county, not the State, may be ordered to pay for a private placement. Bryan, J., concurred in part and dissented in part on whether the court could name the specific facility and therapist; the quote used is from the main (per curiam) opinion. The Alabama Supreme Court denied certiorari and mandamus in Ex parte Montgomery County Department of Human Resources, 10 So. 3d 41 (Ala. 2008), on waiver grounds without reaching the merits, so the Court of Civil Appeals decision stands as the authority.

All twelve authorities named as missing by the verifier were located on CourtListener, retrieved and read; none had to be dropped as unverifiable. Two carried citation errors that are corrected above (In Matter of Lawler is 1986, not 1985; T.L. v. W.C.L. is 203 So. 3d 66, not 208 So. 3d 66), and one is styled differently in the CourtListener cluster (Ex parte Marshall County DHR).

Coverage after this pass: 41 published decisions, every one of the 42 nodes carries between 2 and 6 cases, and no node depends on a single authority. Cranman and Butts were deliberately not mapped to OUT-06, and Butts not to FAIL-02, to keep those nodes at six cases; the doctrine reaches those nodes through Ex parte Watson, Ex parte McClintock, Gowens and Mitchell, which apply it on the facts.

Missing (for a later pass): Harris v. City of Montgomery, 435 So. 2d 1207 (Ala. 1983) — the Alabama Supreme Court decision upholding the constitutionality of the Child Abuse Reporting Act and holding that allegations of tortious conduct beyond the act of reporting (false imprisonment, false arrest, defamation) 'would remove the officer from the purview of § 26-14-9.' It is quoted as controlling in both Brown v. Pound and Gowens, and it is the principal limit on the reporter-immunity cases the brief maps to INP-01, INP-02 and INP-06; without it those nodes state the immunity without its exception.

Missing (for a later pass): Bowman v. State Dep't of Human Resources, 534 So. 2d 304 (Ala. Civ. App. 1988) — the source of the rule, quoted in V.M., that DHR must present 'evidence of recent attempts to locate viable alternatives in order to establish that termination of parental rights is the least drastic alternative.' That recency requirement is the operative test at OUT-02 and ACT-04 and is why Ex parte T.V. and V.M. reverse; the brief uses the rule without citing its origin.

Missing (for a later pass): Crews v. Houston County Dep't of Pensions & Security, 358 So. 2d 451 (Ala. Civ. App. 1978) — the origin of the Alabama right to effective assistance of counsel in a termination case, which Ex parte E.D. quotes and which the brief's own note identifies as the true source of the language its FAIL-01 and OUT-02 practice point relies on. It should be cited rather than described in a footnote.

Missing (for a later pass): W.C. v. State Dep't of Human Resources, 887 So. 2d 251 (Ala. Civ. App. 2003) — the decision T.L. v. W.C.L. quotes for the settled rule that 'the constitutional due process clause does not require the appointment of counsel for an indigent parent in dependency and temporary custody proceedings.' It states the DEC-05 and INP-12 proposition more cleanly than either T.L. or N.G., and its predecessor Morgan v. Lauderdale County Dep't of Pensions & Security, 494 So. 2d 649 (Ala. Civ. App. 1986), is the earlier link in the same chain.

Missing (for a later pass): Ex parte Marshall County Dep't of Human Resources, 233 So. 3d 345 (Ala. 2017) — the Alabama Supreme Court decision in the same litigation as the brief's J.V. v. Marshall County DHR, which the Court of Civil Appeals expressly follows for case designations. A practitioner working INP-04 would expect the higher court's decision in that dispute to be cited, not merely distinguished in a note.

Missing (for a later pass): In re D.M., 738 So. 2d 898 (Ala. Civ. App. 1999) — relied on in Ex parte Montgomery County DHR both for mandamus as the proper vehicle to challenge an order requiring a State agency to pay for a private placement and for the rule that neither § 12-15-71(c)(4) nor § 12-15-70 lets a juvenile court charge a state department with a child's treatment costs. It is the doctrinal predicate for the ACT-03 and ACT-06 payment holding the brief adopts.
